section_summary: This section follows the formation of the Ashida Cabinet, the contest over the premiership after Katayama’s resignation, and proposals for reorganizing Japan’s Foreign Ministry. Later documents cover Labor Minister Kato’s expected resignation and the Showa Denko loan and bribery scandal that brought down the Ashida Cabinet. Enclosures include a loan report, press summaries, and editorials on corruption.

subfiles.title: Formation of the Ashida Cabinet
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports disputes over Cabinet appointments and occupation clearance.
subfiles.summary: The closing page describes objections to Morito and Nagae, clearance of Kurusu’s appointment, and a proposal for two parliamentary vice ministers per ministry.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation: Formation of Ashida Cabinet
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Records Matsumoto Takizo’s account of negotiations and occupation consultations behind the new Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Matsumoto recounts the candidate lists, allocation of ministries among three coalition parties, and disputes over the attorney generalship, finance, agriculture, education, and the Economic Stabilization Board. He says occupation officers raised questions while leaving final selection to the Japanese government. The memorandum also covers Katayama’s refusal of the Foreign Ministry, Kurusu’s delayed assumption of office, and proposed appointments below Cabinet rank.

subfiles.title: The New Ashida Cabinet
subfiles.about: Provides a Cabinet photograph and brief biographies of Ashida’s ministers.
subfiles.summary: The clipping identifies Cabinet members, offices, party affiliations, and career backgrounds.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice for Despatch 263
subfiles.about: Marks the attached despatch copy as the record copy.
subfiles.summary: A filing notice substitutes this copy for an unreturned original action copy.

subfiles.title: Political Factors Surrounding Resignation of Katayama Cabinet and Election of Dr. Ashida Hitoshi as Prime Minister
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes the political contest between Katayama’s resignation and Ashida’s election.
subfiles.summary: Sebald describes party maneuvering, opposition to dissolving the Diet, rival support for Yoshida, and Ashida’s coalition strategy. He assesses Ashida’s position as precarious but potentially sustainable.

subfiles.title: Bill for Establishment and Organization of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a proposed Foreign Ministry organization bill and comments on its provisions.
subfiles.summary: Sebald explains the need for replacement ministry legislation and the proposed ministry’s status under occupation authority. He notes a possible jurisdictional dispute over foreign commerce.

subfiles.title: Bill for Institution of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Defines the organization, functions, and authority of the Foreign Ministry.
subfiles.summary: The bill establishes the ministry and diplomatic establishments, lists responsibilities from foreign policy to repatriation and occupation records, and replaces the earlier organizing ordinance.

subfiles.title: Foreign Ministry Establishment Bill, Japanese text
subfiles.about: Supplies the Japanese text and stated reason for the proposed Foreign Ministry law.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese-language enclosure contains the bill’s articles and an explanation that new legislation is needed with the National Government Organization Law.

subfiles.title: Kato Kanju’s anticipated resignation
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Kato Shizu’s account of her husband’s planned resignation as Labor Minister.
subfiles.summary: Kato Shizu says he intends to resign over government labor policy before the Diet reconvenes.

subfiles.title: Labor Minister Kato’s conditional resignation
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Kato’s views on revisions to the National Public Service Law and his possible resignation.
subfiles.summary: Kato expects to resign if the Cabinet rejects his proposed protections for public workers’ bargaining and strike rights. The airgram links his decision to MacArthur’s July letter and frustration with conservative Cabinet colleagues.

subfiles.title: Ashida Cabinet Resigns Following Arrest of Two Former State Ministers, Dr. Kurusu Takeo and Mr. Nishio Suehiro
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the Cabinet’s resignation amid the Showa Denko bribery investigation.
subfiles.summary: Sebald recounts the arrests of Kurusu and Nishio, describes loans to Showa Denko and allegations involving prominent officials, and summarizes newspaper reactions. He then surveys party negotiations over a successor Cabinet and the prospect of a general election.

subfiles.title: Loans Made to Showa Denko Co., Ltd.
subfiles.about: Documents financing provided to Showa Denko.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese-language report and tables describe Showa Denko’s reconstruction plans, loan applications, financing, and use of funds.

subfiles.title: Summary of Information Prepared by Reconstruction Finance Bank Concerning Loans to Showa Denko
subfiles.about: Tabulates equipment and working-capital loans to Showa Denko.
subfiles.summary: Lists ¥2,384,700,000 in bank loans and ¥440,500,000 in guaranteed syndicate loans.

subfiles.title: Prosecutors Arrest ESB Chief Kurusu
subfiles.from: Tokyo Shimbun, Mainichi, Asahi, Yomiuri, and Jiji Shimpo
subfiles.about: Compiles press accounts of Kurusu’s arrest and the Showa Denko investigation.
subfiles.summary: The compilation describes searches, suspected payments to Kurusu, his relationship with Showa Denko president Hinohara, and the government’s initial response. It also summarizes prosecutors’ statements, disputed loan figures, the company’s reconstruction, and other people drawn into the investigation.

subfiles.title: What Does Showa Scandal Reveal?
subfiles.about: Argues that the Showa Denko case exposes damaging links among politics, finance, and government.
subfiles.summary: The editorial calls for a thorough investigation and warns that repeated corruption scandals erode public confidence and obstruct Japan’s reconstruction.

subfiles.title: Showa Denko Scandal and What It Teaches Us
subfiles.about: Presents a Communist critique of the scandal and reconstruction lending.
subfiles.summary: The editorial attributes the scandal to ties among large companies, banks, politicians, and bureaucrats, and advocates public control of banks and key industries.

subfiles.title: Editorial on corruption in public life
subfiles.about: Discusses corruption allegations involving Diet members and government officials.
subfiles.summary: Calls for thorough investigations while viewing legislative efforts to expose graft as democratic progress.
